title: MVVM (Model-View-ViewModel) Pattern
oneLiner: Exposes observable state and commands from a ViewModel that the View binds to declaratively, eliminating manual UI-update code.

hero.name: The Binder
hero.catchphrase: Change the data, the view updates itself. No manual wiring.
hero.power: Exposes observable state from a ViewModel that the View binds to automatically, so UI updates happen without any manual synchronization code.
hero.weakness: Heavy two-way data binding can make data flow hard to trace — a single change can ripple through bindings in ways that are genuinely difficult to debug.
hero.origin: The Binder appeared after a settings screen had 40 lines of `label.text = model.value` calls scattered everywhere, one for every field, each needing manual updates whenever the underlying data changed.

story.problem: A settings screen has 40 lines of manual `label.text = model.value` calls, one per field, each needing to be re-run any time the underlying data changes. Forgetting one leaves the UI showing stale data.
story.solution: The Binder introduces a `SettingsViewModel` exposing observable properties. The View binds declaratively to those properties — when the ViewModel's data changes, the bound UI elements update themselves automatically.
story.result: The 40 manual update calls disappear entirely. Changing a value in the ViewModel updates every bound UI element instantly, with zero manual wiring.

before: Every data change needs a matching manual UI update call
Forgetting an update call leaves the UI showing stale data
UI update logic is scattered across many call sites
after: The View binds declaratively to ViewModel state
UI elements update automatically when bound data changes
No manual update calls exist anywhere

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: Forty near-identical lines manually copy model values into UI labels, one per field.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I added a new setting and forgot the manual UI update line. It's been showing the wrong value for two days.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Binder appears holding threads that connect data points directly to UI elements, glowing whenever data changes.
panels.speaker: The Binder
panels.dialogue: Stop manually copying values into the UI. Bind the view to the data directly — when the data changes, the view just knows.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: SettingsViewModel exposes observable properties. The View's binding declaration links each label to a property automatically.
panels.speaker: The Binder
panels.dialogue: You never write label.text = value again. Declare the binding once — every future change propagates on its own.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: A new setting binds itself to the UI in one declarative line, no manual update code required.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: The new setting displays correctly automatically. I didn't write a single manual update line for it.

useWhen: Your UI framework provides real data-binding support (React with state, Vue, Angular, WPF, SwiftUI, Compose).
You have many UI elements that need to stay synchronized with underlying data, and manual updates are error-prone.
You want the ViewModel to be independently testable, exposing state and commands without any UI framework dependency.
avoidWhen: The UI framework has no real data-binding support — hand-rolling MVVM's binding machinery yourself is a lot of work for little gain.
The screen is simple enough that manual updates were never actually error-prone.
Complex, deeply chained bindings would make data flow harder to trace than simple, explicit update calls.
commonMistakes: Building deeply chained or bidirectional bindings that make it genuinely hard to trace where a change originated.
Putting business logic (not just presentation state) into the ViewModel, blurring the Model/ViewModel boundary.
Over-relying on two-way binding for things that should be explicit, one-directional data flow (a common source of hard-to-debug UI state bugs).
Confusing MVVM with MVP — MVVM leans on the framework's binding system; MVP relies on explicit method calls through a View interface.
explanation.realWorldExample: WPF and Xamarin's data binding, Vue's reactive `ref()`/`computed()`, and (in spirit) React's state-driven re-rendering are all MVVM or MVVM-adjacent — the View reacts automatically to ViewModel/state changes rather than being manually updated.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Is this basically what React does with state?

conversation.speaker: The Binder
conversation.message: Close in spirit — React's state-driven re-rendering shares my core idea: change the data, the view updates itself. Classic MVVM usually implies more explicit two-way binding frameworks (WPF, Vue), but the philosophy is the same.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What's the real danger of leaning on you too heavily?

conversation.speaker: The Binder
conversation.message: Traceability. With enough chained, two-way bindings, a single UI interaction can ripple through several ViewModels in ways that are genuinely hard to follow when something goes wrong.

codeBattle.scenario: Your desktop app built with a framework supporting real data binding has dozens of manual `updateLabel()` calls scattered throughout the codebase, and UI elements regularly show stale data because someone forgot to call the right update function.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Binder replaces manual update calls with declarative bindings to observable ViewModel state, so the UI updates itself automatically whenever the data changes.

quiz.question: What does the View do in MVVM, that it doesn't do in MVP?
options: It binds declaratively to the ViewModel's observable state, updating automatically without explicit method calls
It contains all the business logic
It has no relationship to the ViewModel at all
quiz.answer: It binds declaratively to the ViewModel's observable state, updating automatically without explicit method calls
quiz.explanation: Declarative, automatic binding is exactly what distinguishes MVVM's View from MVP's explicitly-instructed View.

quiz.question: What problem does MVVM's data binding eliminate?
options: Manual, error-prone synchronization code between data and UI elements
The need for any data model at all
The need for a View entirely
quiz.answer: Manual, error-prone synchronization code between data and UI elements
quiz.explanation: Binding removes the exact class of bug where a manual UI-update call is forgotten, leaving stale data displayed.

quiz.question: What's a real risk of heavy two-way data binding in MVVM?
options: Data flow can become genuinely hard to trace when a change ripples through chained bindings
It always makes the application faster
It removes the need for any state management
It cannot be tested at all
quiz.answer: Data flow can become genuinely hard to trace when a change ripples through chained bindings
quiz.explanation: The convenience of automatic propagation comes at the cost of sometimes-opaque data flow, especially with bidirectional bindings.

quiz.question: What's a real-world framework built around MVVM-style binding?
quiz.explanation: WPF's binding system is one of the most direct, well-known real-world implementations of the MVVM pattern.
